question: Which of the foundational TBML techniques identified in the 2006 FATF report does NOT depend on misrepresenting the price of the goods, and how do criminals use several financial institutions to keep it from being spotted?
summary: Of the foundational TBML techniques traced back to the FATF 2006 study, multiple invoicing is the one whose description does not turn on the price stated for the goods: it works by issuing more than one invoice for the same goods, so the seller can justify receiving multiple payments. Industry guidance (Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT) notes explicitly that this will be harder to detect if the colluding parties use more than one financial institution to facilitate the payments. By contrast, over- and under-invoicing are defined by misrepresenting the price of the good or service in order to transfer value. Guidance also notes that these techniques are combined in practice (e.g. multiple invoices used alongside phantom shipping) and that no single authority or organisation has full sight of the threat.

drafts.question: Which of the foundational TBML techniques identified in the 2006 FATF report does NOT depend on misrepresenting the price of the goods, and how do criminals use several financial institutions to keep it from being spotted?
drafts.summary: The odd one out is multiple invoicing. Unlike over- and under-invoicing — whose defining feature, per FATF, is misrepresenting the price of the good or service to transfer value — multiple invoicing works by issuing more than one invoice for the same goods, allowing the seller to justify receiving several payments for a single shipment. The stated price can be perfectly genuine; it is the duplication of the payment leg that moves the illicit value. Detection depends on someone noticing that the same shipment has been paid for repeatedly, so launderers spread the duplicate invoices and payments across more than one financial institution: each bank sees only one apparently normal, well-documented trade payment, and no institution has sight of the full set. The Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT Trade Finance Principles note this explicitly, and add that value-misrepresentation generally cannot be identified from trade documents alone, since most goods lack publicly available market prices. FATF also observes that these 2006-era techniques are routinely combined — e.g. multiple invoices layered on top of phantom shipments.

claims.text: The FATF 2006 report identified several techniques that form the foundation of TBML, including over- and under-invoicing of goods and services, whose key element is the misrepresentation of the price of the good or service in order to transfer value, with importer and exporter complicit in the misrepresentation.

Multiple invoicing is the foundational technique that does not rely on misstating price: by issuing more than one invoice for the same goods, a seller can justify the receipt of multiple payments for a single shipment, so the invoiced unit price can be entirely accurate.

Multiple invoicing is harder to detect if the colluding parties use more than one financial institution to facilitate the payments, since no single institution sees the full set of duplicate payments.

Techniques such as over/under invoicing rely on collusion between buyer and seller, and financial institutions generally cannot determine whether misrepresentation of value exists from the trade documents alone, because most products are not traded in public markets and there are no publicly available market prices.

In practice criminals mix these foundational techniques within one scheme; for example, sophisticated ML networks may use phantom shipping in conjunction with multiple invoices, with an initial shipment of real goods providing a veneer of legitimacy and subsequent trades using multiple invoices for phantom shipments as cover for fund transfers.
The techniques first identified in the 2006 FATF study continue to be exploited because they are highly flexible and adaptable despite changes in global trading patterns.
